scenes.text: Last time, an average hid a group that was doing much worse. So what would fix it? Here's one attempt. A government opens a free skin cancer screening clinic. It's open from nine to four on weekdays, in the centre of a large regional town, and it's genuinely free to everyone. Who won't use it? And is it fair? By the end, you'll be able to answer both, without using the words lazy or choice.

Two words sit at the centre of this, and they're easy to mix up. Equality means everyone gets the same. Equity means everyone gets what they need to reach a similar outcome. Suppose a state gives every school the same ten thousand dollars for a health program. That's equality. A school where students already eat well and see a doctor turns it into a small gain. But a school where a third of students skip meals, and the nearest clinic is an hour away, needs different things first. Same money, different starting points, and the gap gets wider.

One careful point. Not every difference in health is unfair. Older people have more chronic disease than younger people, and nobody could remove that difference completely. A difference counts as an inequity only when it passes three tests. It's avoidable, it's unnecessary, and it's unfair. Showing that a gap passes those three tests is part of your argument. Don't just assume it.

Now access. A service that exists isn't the same as a service you can use. There are at least six kinds of barrier. Financial, which isn't just the fee, it's lost wages, petrol and childcare too. Geographic, the distance, and whether a bus runs when the service is open. Cultural, whether the service feels safe and respectful to your community. Language and literacy. Physical, whether the building works for people with disability. And informational, whether people even know it exists.

Back to the clinic. Free handles the fee, but not the lost wages of coming during work hours, because it's only open while most people are at work. It's in one town, with no interpreter mentioned, and no sign of how anyone hears about it. That's five of the six barriers untouched, and the financial one only half fixed. This is a classic exam trap. A question about access almost always gives you a free service. The word free is bait. Name at least three kinds of barrier, and say which ones the case actually fixes.

Participation means the people affected help design, run and judge what happens to them. It's not a courtesy. It changes whether a program works, for three reasons. Communities know their own barriers, like a bus that doesn't run at four. A service people helped build is one they trust, and trust is what gets people through the door. And it changes what counts as success. That's why community-controlled health services, run by the communities they serve, are often more trusted and better used. But watch for the fake. Asking for comments on a plan that's already finished is consultation, not participation.

A right is an entitlement you hold because you're a person. The same World Health Organization constitution you met earlier says the highest attainable standard of health is a fundamental right of every human being. So care can't depend on whether someone seems to deserve it, like a smoker with lung disease, or a driver hurt while speeding. Two limits keep this honest. A right doesn't mean unlimited resources. And a right on paper, with no access, isn't yet a right in practice.

So how do these principles actually improve health status? Here's the mechanism. The group furthest behind carries the most ill health that could be avoided. When help is matched to what that group needs, the same effort removes far more ill health there than in a group that's already close to the best it can be. So equity isn't just fair. It's often one of the most effective ways to lift a whole population. And the four work as a chain. A right nobody can reach changes nothing, and a service nobody trusts doesn't get used.
Two things to remember. A difference becomes an inequity when it's avoidable, unnecessary and unfair. And free isn't the same as accessible, so check all six gates.

Two exam questions. First. A hospital's diabetes education materials are only available in English, in a district where a quarter of residents speak another language at home. Identify the social justice principle most clearly breached, and propose one change that would address it. Pause here to answer.

It's access, through a language and literacy barrier. The materials exist, but a quarter of the district can't use them. A good change is translating them into the main community languages, or providing interpreters at education sessions, ideally designed with those communities. The classic mistake is calling it equality, just because everyone gets the same leaflet.
Second. Explain how the social justice principle of equity can improve the health status of a community. Pause here to answer.

Define equity against equality first. Then give the mechanism: the group furthest behind has the most avoidable ill health, so help matched to its needs removes the most, and the community's health status rises furthest. Finish by linking to access, because targeted help still needs to be reachable. The classic mistake is arguing that equity is fair, and stopping there.

So, to judge any health initiative, ask four questions. Is it treated as a right? Is help shared by need? Can people actually reach it? And did the people affected help decide? But why do some groups start so far behind in the first place? Next, we'll follow the chain of causes that comes before the gates.
